transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-09-15 14:00 PDT | Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Brooks (Redwood SE), John Reyes (CISO - Lumen Financial), Maya Chen (Cloud Architect), Carlos Ruiz (Network Engineer)

--- Summary ---
(automated summary may be imperfect) Deep dive on private VPC and on-prem security for Redwood deployments. Focus on network isolation, SSO, audit logs, KMS, and SOC 2 evidence.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Samira Patel from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account. With me is Ethan Brooks, our security SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] John: Good, thanks. John Reyes here, CISO at Lumen. We have Maya and Carlos on as well.
[00:12] Maya: Hi all.
[00:13] Carlos: Morning.
[00:15] Samira: Quick agenda \u2014 SOC 2/ISO controls mapping, SSO and RBAC, audit logs and SIEM integration, encryption/KMS, then deep dive on VPC topology, ingress/egress and firewall rules, and then next steps. Sound ok?
[00:27] John: Yep, that's perfect. Our main ask is to validate we can run Redwood in our VPC with no internet egress except where we explicitly allow it and to understand how keys and logs are handled for compliance.
[00:38] Ethan: Great. I'll start with the high level: Redwood Private can be deployed into a customer-managed VPC or on-prem in an air-gapped fashion. For the VPC option we support private endpoints, we can set up our control-plane peering (or a dedicated management VPC) but all inference planes live in your subnets.
[00:54] Maya: When you say control plane peering \u2014 what traffic goes over that? We need to limit anything that touches cardholder data zones.
[01:01] Ethan: Good call. Control plane is only used for management metadata and deployment orchestration. It does not pass PII or model inputs by default, we can configure the control channel to use a dedicated management VPC that has very restricted routes. If you need, we can also support customer-managed endpoints for management APIs so traffic never leaves your network.
[01:20] Carlos: So inference traffic \u2014 tokens, prompts, responses \u2014 that stays in our private subnets?
[01:24] Ethan: Yes. Compute nodes sit in your subnets. By default no public IPs, NAT gateways only for explicit egress. We do recommend explicit egress rules to allowed destinations for things like OS package updates or image pulls. For fully air-gapped on-prem we'll provide a bundle and offline artifacts.
[01:41] John: Ok, and what about KMS? We have customer-managed KMS (AWS KMS with custom keys) and we'd prefer keys to never be accessible outside Lumen.
[01:50] Ethan: We support both: integrate with your cloud KMS with key policies scoped to the VPC and roles, or for higher assurance we support HSM-backed keys or KMS proxying through the customer network. In the VPC model the encryption keys never leave your account \u2014 Redwood's runtime can call KMS through an IAM role in your account, or we can use an on-prem HSM where keys are never exported.
[02:12] Maya: Do you have docs on key rotation and audit evidence for encryption? That's a SOC 2 point for us.
[02:18] Samira: Yes \u2014 Ethan will share the KMS integration guide and rotation docs. We also include KMS operation logs as part of the audit artifact set.
[02:26] Ethan: We'll include example CloudTrail events and how to surface them in Splunk or Datadog.
[02:31] John: Good. Another big one is SSO and RBAC. We use Okta and have role mappings to AD groups. How do you map SAML entitlements to Redwood roles?
[02:40] Ethan: We support SAML 2.0, SCIM provisioning, and granular RBAC. You can map Okta groups to Redwood roles (admin, devops, observer, etc.). We can also sync groups via SCIM so users are auto-provisioned and de-provisioned.
[02:54] Carlos: Is there an audit trail for who called what model, and token counts for chargeback? We need per-user logs for billing and forensic.
[03:02] Ethan: Yes \u2014 request-level logs capture user identity, route, model version, token counts, latencies. Logs can be forwarded to your SIEM in near-real time via secure delivery (TLS) or pushed to an S3 bucket in your account for retention.
[03:16] Maya: What about PII redaction and ability to exclude certain fields from logs?
[03:20] Ethan: We have configurable redaction rules and also can disable request content logging if you prefer. You'd still get metadata \u2014 user id, token counts, timestamps \u2014 without the prompt text. That's common for PCI/PHI scenarios.
[03:33] John: Ok. On the network side \u2014 ingress, egress \u2014 we need specifics: recommended subnet layout, NACLs, firewall rules, ports, and how to do deep packet inspection if we need it.
[03:45] Ethan: Sure. Typical layout: management subnets for control plane endpoints, compute subnets for inference nodes, and storage subnets for model artifacts and object storage. No public IPs on compute. NACLs deny by default, allow only required control-plane CIDRs and your admin IP ranges. Firewall: we recommend limiting egress to your artifact registries and your KMS endpoints. For egress inspection you can place a proxy or IDS/IPS in the egress path \u2014 we support routing via an egress NAT + inspection appliance.
[04:12] Carlos: Do you support service chaining to our Palo Alto/Check Point devices?
[04:15] Ethan: Yes \u2014 if you provide a transit gateway or equivalent, we can route egress through your firewall cluster. We also support static routes for direct peering so traffic flows through your security appliances.
[04:25] Maya: What ports are required?
[04:27] Ethan: Management plane uses HTTPS 443. For internal node-to-node we use gRPC over 7001-7010 by default (configurable), and for container runtime management we need SSH to the bastion only \u2014 we avoid opening SSH to all compute nodes. Model artifact pulls use standard HTTPS to your S3 endpoints or registry.
[04:46] Samira: Quick note, some of our docs mention port 50051 for gRPC in older versions; sorry for the inconsistency in docs, we'll include the current port list in the diagram.
[04:55] John: Good call. Another question \u2014 audit log retention. SOC 2 auditors will want 12 months of immutable logs. Can you push logs to our S3 with object lock/immute?
[05:04] Ethan: Yes, we can deliver logs to your S3 and you can enable object lock and bucket policies for immutability. We also provide signed delivery manifests so you can prove chain of custody.
[05:14] Carlos: We use Splunk on-prem. Can you forward events to our Splunk HEC endpoint over TLS?
[05:20] Ethan: Absolutely, Splunk HEC is supported. We can also batch-deliver to S3 then you can ingest.
[05:26] Maya: About data residency \u2014 some regulated workloads must stay in EU regions. Can you ensure model serving is restricted to a region?
[05:33] Ethan: Yes, you can pin model versions and routing policies to specific regions and AZs. For Private VPC we deploy in your chosen region only. For multi-region high availability we provision replicas in specified regions \u2014 you control the placement.
[05:47] John: Are there any telemetry callbacks to Redwood's hosted systems that might leak metadata?
[05:53] Ethan: By default, no prompt-level data is sent to Redwood's multi-tenant hosted catalog. We do send anonymized metrics for product telemetry unless disabled. For enterprise customers we offer a mode that disables product telemetry and routes control-plane traffic through your management VPC.
[06:10] John: Ok. On firewalling, we need a sample ACL or set of iptables rules we can present to our network team.
[06:16] Samira: We'll include a sample iptables and NSG rule set. Ethan, can you capture the minimal allow-list for us?
[06:21] Ethan: Yep \u2014 I'll compile a minimal allow-list: control-plane CIDRs, KMS endpoints, artifact registries, SIEM endpoints, internal service ports.
[06:31] Maya: For on-prem air-gapped, how do you do model updates and security patches?
[06:36] Ethan: For air-gapped customers we provide signed artifact bundles via secure transfer. Patches are delivered as signed packages you can ingest offline. We also support an update appliance that you place on your network to pull from an internal mirror.
[06:48] Carlos: About RBAC \u2014 can we tie actions to AD groups such that only a small Admin group can call certain high-capacity models? We need to limit cost/spend and exposure.
[06:56] Ethan: Yes \u2014 role-based quotas and per-route permissions are supported. You can restrict model variants to certain groups and set token quotas and hard limits per role.
[07:07] John: Great. A nit \u2014 our auditors also ask for proof of pen-test and vuln scans. Do you provide attestation?
[07:14] Samira: We maintain a SOC 2 report and annual penetration test summary; we can share redacted reports under NDA. We also have a public vulnerability disclosure policy.
[07:23] John: Ok.
[07:24] Maya: On the logging format \u2014 is there a canonical schema? Our SIEM team prefers JSON with fields: timestamp, user_id, action, model, prompt_hash, token_count, request_id.
[07:33] Ethan: Yes we emit JSON logs with those fields and we can add custom fields you require. Prompt_hash is included for dedupe without storing full content, when content logging is disabled.
[07:45] Carlos: What about network segmentation between tenants \u2014 we have several business units and need hard tenancy separation in some cases.
[07:53] Ethan: In the Dedicated/Private offering each customer can have isolated clusters. Within your account, we can create separate subnets and security groups per BU; for absolute separation we recommend separate clusters per BU.
[08:05] John: Can we get a walk-through of the firewalling and ingress/egress diagrams?
[08:09] Ethan: Sure, I'm pulling up the diagram now \u2014 (screen share) so here's management VPC, here's the compute subnets, here's the egress NAT and the optional inspection appliance. You route your egress through the appliance, and we only open 443 outbound to your artifact repos and KMS.
[08:27] Speaker 6: (unlabeled) can you repeat the KMS flow?
[08:30] Ethan: Sure: Redwood runtime assumes a role in your account, then calls KMS to decrypt model keys on-demand. Private keys never leave KMS; decrypted data is held only in memory on the node. For HSM, the runtime sends a signing/decrypt request to the HSM over your internal network \u2014 keys are not exportable.
[08:53] Maya: Any guidance on securing EC2 metadata endpoints?
[08:56] Ethan: We recommend IMDSv2 and we enforce instance metadata protection. Also we run the runtime with least privilege IAM roles and short-lived credentials.
[09:05] John: Alright, let's flag a couple of open items: egress inspection path and whether telemetry can be fully disabled.
[09:11] Samira: We'll confirm telemetry disable mode in writing and show the config. Also we'll document the egress inspection patterns and example ACLs.
[09:19] Maya: For the pilot, we want to run a model inside our VPC and exercise SIEM ingestion and KMS integration. Are there quotas or throttles we should know about?
[09:28] Ethan: For Dedicated/Private pilot we can provision a small cluster sized for your test load; we'll provide expected throughput and token limits. We also have soft quotas we can raise for pilots.
[09:38] Carlos: For the on-prem appliance, what hypervisor support do you need?
[09:42] Ethan: We support VMware ESXi and KVM-based installs. We can provide OVA images and a containerized bundle.
[09:49] John: Good. Any unexpected dependencies?
[09:51] Ethan: Only that you provide the KMS endpoint, SIEM endpoints, and artifact registry access; and if you want peering through a transit gateway, that config needs to be in place.
[10:00] Samira: Great. We'll follow up with a package: VPC diagram, minimal allow-list, KMS integration guide, audit log schema, and the proposal for the pilot.
[10:09] John: Perfect. Last question \u2014 does Redwood maintain an inventory of third-party libraries and versions for SBOM?
[10:16] Ethan: Yes, we can provide an SBOM and vulnerability scan results.
[10:20] Maya: Thanks everyone.
[10:22] Carlos: Thanks.
[10:23] Samira: Thanks all, we'll send notes and docs.
